transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-05
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 40 minutes
Location: Zoom recording / record ID fb-2025-10-05-001
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jamal Ortiz (Producer / SE), Samantha Lee (BlueHarbor - Head of Product), Carlos Ruiz (BlueHarbor - CMO)
Links: Draft show notes: https://redwood.ai/docs/blueharbor-notes, Slide deck reference: https://redwood.ai/decks/blueharbor-podcast.pdf

Summary:
Quick podcast-style interview with BlueHarbor about their use of Redwood Inference for personalized content generation in marketing workflows; conversation covers integration story, performance and cost tradeoffs, and the business impact.

Topics:
- BlueHarbor product use case and goal
- Integration timeline and engineering work
- Latency, cost, and reliability tradeoffs
- Security controls and enterprise requirements
- Marketing outcomes and metrics

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Alright, welcome everyone, uh, this is Maya from Redwood, thanks so much for joining. Uh, we're doing a recorded podcast style chat, so we'll jump in - Jamal is here helping with audio and notes.
[00:18] Jamal: Hey everyone, quick mic check, can you hear me?
[00:22] Samantha: Yep, loud and clear. Excited to be here.
[00:25] Carlos: Hi all, thanks for having us.
[00:30] Maya: Great. So maybe to kick off, Samantha, can you give a quick, like 2 minute overview of BlueHarbor and what you guys are building?
[00:40] Samantha: Yeah for sure, um BlueHarbor is a marketing automation platform, focused on mid-market e-commerce, we do personalized email, landing pages, product descriptions, and we've been using Redwood to generate copy at scale. We started exploring LLMs last year, and it got to the point where commercial APIs were either too expensive or lacked the reliability we need, so we looked at Redwood for predictability and the dedicated routing stuff.
[01:08] Maya: Nice. And Carlos, what's the business signal that made this project a priority?
[01:14] Carlos: For us it was conversion. We saw a 12% lift in A/B tests with more personalized product descriptions; the problem was the cost per token and spikes in latency during peak sends. We needed a partner that could give us consistent latency at high throughput.
[01:34] Jamal: Quick plug - there was some initial benchmarking we ran with Redwood Dedicated where we saw, I think, average p95 latencies at like 180 to 220 ms for 512 token generations, memory depending. Might have said that wrong in the deck.
[01:55] Samantha: Yeah that lined up with our tests. There was some fun stuff with the KV cache - we had to tune prefix caching, it, it helped a lot.
[02:10] Maya: Love that. Let's dig into the integration a bit - engineering work, timeline, and who on your team did the heavy lifting?
[02:18] Samantha: Our platform team did it, two engineers over about four sprints. Most work was around request routing and templateization, and also managing the KMS integration for customer data encryption. We did a private deployment in our VPC, so there were a couple of network quirks with our firewall rules.
[02:38] Carlos: One thing to flag - the Redwood docs on the private control plane were super helpful, quick shoutout.
[02:45] Maya: Nice. On the security side, I remember we had some questions around audit logs and SSO. Did the SAML flow work smoothly?
[02:52] Samantha: It did, although there were a few steps where, uh, the sample - I mean SAML configurations - the identity team asked for more explicit certificate rotation docs. Jamal helped with that.
[03:05] Jamal: Yep, we shipped a step-by-step and a sample script, though a few names in the docs got munged in an earlier version.
[03:12] Maya: Classic. Switching gears - any surprises on performance or quality once you went to production?
[03:18] Samantha: We did see that batching settings mattered a lot. Initially we prioritized latency and disabled batching, but during big sends that killed throughput and raised costs. So the tradeoff was, uh, we tuned a medium batch size and used prefix caching for the most common templates. That hit our latency SLOs and reduced token usage.
[03:41] Carlos: We also leveraged quantized model variants for the bulk of non-creative copy, saved a lot on GPU hours.
[03:49] Maya: When you say quantized, were you talking about the open model variants Redwood recommended or customer-trained models?
[03:55] Samantha: Mostly the open variants from the Redwood catalog, combined with some in-house fine-tuning for brand voice.
[04:03] Maya: Got it. How about cost - were the economics what you expected?
[04:08] Carlos: Better than expected once we applied batching and cache rules. Our per-email generation cost dropped by around 40% versus initial POC numbers.
[04:18] Maya: Love that. For listeners who care about privacy/regulatory, how did data residency and KMS play out?
[04:25] Samantha: We had some EU customers so we chose a private deployment in the EU region, used customer-managed KMS keys, and retained audit logs for 6 months, which answered legal's concerns.
[04:38] Jamal: There was a small hiccup with log retention settings showing up late in the console but we pushed a fix.
[04:45] Samantha: Yeah, Jamal saved us there.
[04:48] Maya: On the marketing side - Carlos, what outputs have you seen? Any metrics you can share for the episode?
[04:55] Carlos: Sure, we saw a 12% lift in product page conversions for pages where we replaced generic copy with Redwood-generated personalized descriptions, and email open rates improved by about 6% with dynamic subject lines. Those numbers helped justify the Dedicated capacity spend.
[05:12] Maya: That's awesome. Any favorite anecdotes from customers about the content?
[05:16] Samantha: One of our retailers ran a flash sale and used dynamically generated product blurbs; they reported an immediate uptick in AOV, which was a nice win.
[05:25] Maya: Nice. Ok let's go a little technical for the audience - Jamal, can you explain the serving setup in plain terms?
[05:31] Jamal: Yeah, so think of Redwood Dedicated as a reserved pool of GPU instances that take requests routed through a control plane. We do continuous batching, prefix/KV caching so repeated contexts are fast, and there's a router that can fall back to hosted endpoints if the Dedicated pool saturates. Sometimes the transcript will say K V cache spelled out which is annoying but that's the tech.
[05:53] Maya: And the failover - you mentioned auto fallback - did you ever need it in production?
[05:58] Samantha: A couple times during big sends we saw fallback kick in for a small percentage of requests; the application handled it gracefully and we didn't see user impact.
[06:08] Carlos: It did highlight the importance of consistent model variants across tiers though, so predictions stayed aligned.
[06:16] Maya: For teams thinking about starting a pilot, what would you recommend as the first experiment?
[06:22] Samantha: Start with subject lines and short product blurbs, something where you can A/B test quickly. Keep latency SLOs conservative at first and measure cost impact with a small traffic slice.
[06:32] Maya: Great advice. Any challenging conversations with procurement or legal we should mention?
[06:37] Carlos: Procurement wanted strict SLAs around uptime and incident response; Redwood's enterprise package and the Dedicated contract helped close that. Legal pushed on data retention and export controls, which we solved with the private deployment + KMS.
[06:52] Jamal: There were also some questions about SSO role mapping - that took a short config session.
[06:58] Samantha: And one minor thing - some internal docs referenced an old model name, so we had to update the runbook.
[07:05] Maya: Haha, runbook updates are always fun. Okay, switching to the audience-facing story - what messaging resonated most when you promoted this?
[07:13] Carlos: That it was "predictable performance at scale" - customers care more about consistent page loads and batch sends than raw bench numbers.
[07:21] Samantha: Also emphasizing brand voice control was important, because marketing teams worry about tone and hallucinations.
[07:29] Maya: Speaking of hallucinations, any incidents?
[07:32] Samantha: One time a generated blurb had a factual error about a product spec; we added a validation step in the pipeline to flag any factual assertions and send to a human reviewer for high-value SKUs.
[07:46] Maya: Smart. For the podcast audience - what would you say the top three learnings are?
[07:49] Carlos: 1) Start small with A/B tests; 2) Invest in caching and batching to control costs; 3) Make sure your identity and audit needs are covered early.
[07:58] Samantha: I'd add: 4) Keep a human-in-the-loop for critical content.
[08:03] Maya: Great. We're about 8 minutes in - actually, listener note, we're at about 40 minutes total but we'll do some shorter segments for the final edit. Jamal, any notes on audio?
[08:12] Jamal: Levels look good, I might trim a couple of long pauses.
[08:16] Maya: Cool. Quick off-script question - did you ever test any reranking or embedding features for search?
[08:22] Samantha: We did a small pilot using embeddings for semantic search on knowledge base articles, that reduced helpdesk deflection by about 9%.
[08:31] Carlos: The embeddings were hosted on Redwood managed endpoints, which made the integration straightforward.
[08:37] Maya: Perfect. All right, last couple of questions - any vendor comparisons you did that would be useful for listeners?
[08:44] Samantha: We ran comparisons against OpenAI and a couple of open-source stacks - the main differentiator was cost predictability and private deployment options. OpenAI had strong model quality out of the box but the cost and rate limits made it tricky at scale.
[09:02] Carlos: Also Anthropic came up in some hoops, but we preferred Redwood's operational tooling for batching and rollback.
[09:10] Maya: Helpful context. Okay I'm going to do a quick recap of bullets for the show notes and then we'll wrap - anything else to add?
[09:19] Samantha: Just that the partnership was more collaborative than we expected; Redwood's SEs sat with our engineers during the first deploy which sped things up.
[09:28] Maya: Awesome. Carlos?
[09:30] Carlos: Nothing else, thanks for having us. Looking forward to the edit.
[09:34] Maya: Cool - recap of next steps, we'll send the raw audio and draft transcript, Jamal will push edits, Carlos to approve quotes, all by the dates in the action items.
[09:46] Jamal: Noted.
[09:47] Maya: Great. Thanks again, everyone. We'll cut the recording here.
[09:52] [Recording stopped]
